aors.name: U.S. Central Command
aors.threat_profile: Highest OPTEMPO for one-way attack UAS and Group 1-3 ISR threats. Iranian-aligned proxy employment of Shahed-class OWA and quadcopter FPV against fixed sites and maritime assets. GPS jamming and spoofing routine. Gulf reporting suggests a larger share of drones penetrate defenses than ballistic missiles.
aors.operating_notes: Systems require MIL-STD-810 heat and dust tolerance above 50C. GNSS-denied navigation strongly preferred. Sustained engagement volume makes cost per intercept the decisive metric, not single-shot performance.
aors.exchange_context: Shahed-class threats are estimated at $30-50K each. Any effector above roughly $100K per engagement loses the exchange at CENTCOM engagement rates. Merops-class interceptors at $15K have reportedly returned better than 10:1.

aors.name: U.S. European Command
aors.threat_profile: Peer EW threat informed by Ukraine lessons. FPV, Lancet-class loitering munitions, Orlan-class ISR, and Shahed-class OWA at scale. Russia reportedly launched over 54,000 Shahed-type drones by early 2026. Dense friendly airspace deconfliction burden.
aors.operating_notes: Assume full GNSS denial and active RF jamming. Fiber-optic and autonomous terminal guidance defeat RF-only systems. Cold soak to -30C for the northern flank. Highest engagement volume of any AOR, so magazine depth and replenishment rate dominate.
aors.exchange_context: Threat mix skews cheaper than CENTCOM, with many FPV rounds under $5K. Only T0 and T1 effectors hold a favorable exchange against the low end. European LEAP initiative and NATO interceptor procurement are driving prices down further.

aors.name: U.S. Indo-Pacific Command
aors.threat_profile: Peer maritime threat with Group 3-5 ISR-T and armed UAS. Long over-water engagement ranges. Distributed operations across austere island sites with thin logistics.
aors.operating_notes: Salt fog corrosion resistance and maritime clutter rejection required. Long range and endurance dominate the trade space and often exclude the cheapest airframes outright. Expeditionary SWaP limits driven by connector lift.
aors.exchange_context: Higher-value threats tolerate a more expensive effector, so exchange ratio is less binding than in EUCOM. The binding constraint is resupply: an interceptor that cannot be produced or stored forward is unavailable regardless of price. Favor in-theater additive manufacturing and low-cube systems.

aors.name: U.S. Africa Command
aors.threat_profile: VEO employment of commercial Group 1-2 quadcopters for ISR and improvised attack. Low-density threat but austere basing with minimal sustainment reach-back.
aors.operating_notes: Simplicity and maintainability dominate. Systems must operate with small teams, generator power, and infrequent resupply. Low unit cost is decisive because no depot tail exists.
aors.exchange_context: Threats are commercial airframes costing a few thousand dollars. Nothing above T1 holds a favorable exchange. Reusable jammers and smart optics win on cost per engagement because their effector is essentially free.

aors.name: U.S. Southern Command
aors.threat_profile: TCO narco-trafficking UAS for smuggling, surveillance of security forces, and occasional attack. Predominantly commercial Group 1 platforms with growing Group 2 fixed-wing use.
aors.operating_notes: Humidity and jungle canopy degrade EO/IR and RF detection. Passive RF detection is effective against commercial C2 links. Partner-nation interoperability and low training burden preferred.
aors.exchange_context: Cheapest threat set in any AOR at a few thousand dollars per airframe. Kinetic interceptors almost never justify their cost here. Reusable EW and detection-led interdiction are the economically rational answer.

aors.name: U.S. Northern Command
aors.threat_profile: Homeland defense against careless, criminal, and state-sponsored Group 1-2 incursions over installations and critical infrastructure. Legal authorities under 10 USC 130i constrain kinetic and EW defeat.
aors.operating_notes: Spectrum use requires FCC and NTIA coordination. Kinetic defeat over populated areas is largely prohibited. Detect-track-identify performance and low-collateral defeat mechanisms dominate selection.
aors.exchange_context: Cost exchange is nearly irrelevant here because engagement volume is low and legal constraints, not economics, drive selection. Reusable and recoverable systems are preferred for forensic value. Attritable kinetic rounds are usually not employable at all.
